# Results — Study 494 (Bullish Percent Index)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the BPI
calls tops and bottoms: when breadth is washed out (BPI < 30) the index is oversold and
bounces** — encoded as a mechanical rule. BPI is the **percentage of the basket trading above
its 50-day SMA** (a transparent proxy for the classic P&F-buy-signal count); a long fires on the
bar where BPI **crosses up** through 30, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and
we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return on SPY. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes; SPY traded, breadth from **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| BPI proxy | % of the 4-member basket above its **50-day SMA**; range 0..100, mean **68.2**, 27.6% of days < 30, 66.7% > 70 |
| Entries | **159** mechanical oversold up-crosses (BPI through 30) |
| Timing / costs | causal SMA (no look-ahead); cross read on close of *t*, enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per cross |

> **Breadth is a proxy.** True BPI counts every member of a *full exchange* on a Point & Figure
> buy signal. We approximate it with the % of a small surviving ETF basket above its moving
> average — a coarse stand-in that **caps** the test. The Signal axis question is unchanged:
> does the breadth signal beat random-day entries on SPY? Survivorship and the proxy affect only
> the drift baseline, which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes.

## The signal — oversold-cross buy vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch cross-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = cross − random.

| horizon | n | cross | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 159 | −8.6 bps  | 57% | −0.41 | +18.6 bps | **−27.2 bps** | −10.6 bps | −1.00 | 0.318 |
| 10-day | 159 | +37.0 bps | 66% | +1.07 | +33.8 bps | **+3.2 bps**  | +35.0 bps | +0.08 | 0.933 |
| 20-day | 159 | +37.0 bps | 67% | +0.53 | +82.6 bps | **−45.5 bps** | +35.0 bps | −0.83 | 0.406 |
| 60-day | 158 | +207.5 bps| 72% | +1.72 | +209.1 bps| **−1.6 bps**  | +205.5 bps| −0.02 | 0.984 |

Read it carefully. Even the one-sample *t* against zero barely registers (**+0.53** at 20 days,
**+1.72** at 60) — the oversold-cross fires too rarely (159 trades) to ride much drift. Against
the **drift-matched random baseline**, the cross is *worse* at 5/20 days and a dead heat at
10/60 (Δ = −27.2 / +3.2 / −45.5 / −1.6 bps). The cross-minus-random difference **never clears
the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** — the largest Welch *t* is **+0.08** at 10 days (*p* = 0.93). The BPI
does not forecast turns.

## Level rule (BPI < 30, first of run) — same story

The simpler "buy while oversold" reading fares no better against random: Δ = +9.6 / +1.8 /
**−70.2** / +26.3 bps at 5/10/20/60d, none significant (one-sample *t* peaks at +1.94 at 60d,
which is again just drift). Neither the cross nor the level rule beats a dart.

## Per-instrument (H = 20) — the cross loses to random everywhere

The same breadth BPI signal, applied to each tradable tape:

| ticker | entries | cross | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (cross−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 159 | +37.0 bps | +0.53 | +82.6 bps | **−45.5 bps** |
| QQQ | 159 | +71.9 bps | +0.98 | +138.6 bps | **−66.7 bps** |
| IWM | 159 | +49.9 bps | +0.60 | +64.1 bps | **−14.2 bps** |
| DIA | 159 | +38.8 bps | +0.60 | +70.0 bps | **−31.2 bps** |
| GLD | 159 | +63.3 bps | +1.53 | +88.4 bps | **−25.1 bps** |

The oversold-cross **underperforms a dart-throwing entry in 5 of 5 names**. No coherent
cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled drift.

## Breadth-timing placebo — scramble the BPI, nothing changes

The decisive "does the breadth timing matter?" test: block-shuffle the BPI series in time
(blocks of 21 days), keeping its marginal but destroying its alignment with the SPY path, so the
oversold cross fires on dates unrelated to the real breadth. If price genuinely turned on
*washed-out breadth*, the scramble would collapse the result.

| test | observed cross 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-breadth | +37.0 bps | **0.974** | 500 |

**97% of time-scrambled breadth series match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.974). The breadth
timing carries no information — a randomly re-timed BPI does just as well. "BPI calls bottoms" is
busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real bounce

On a deterministic tape where a common breadth factor drives the members *and* an upward bounce
is **planted** whenever breadth is deeply oversold (knob `edge`), the same oversold-cross rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | cross | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 141 | +4.2 bps | 53% | +0.08 |
| **0.60** (real planted bounce) | 141 | +472.7 bps | 65% | **+3.38** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted
breadth-bounce lights up at *t* = +3.38 with a 65% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The oversold-cross buy does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (cross − random = −27.2 / +3.2 / −45.5 / −1.6 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the cross-vs-random
  Welch *t* never clears 2, max +0.08 at 10 days, *p* = 0.93). The level rule is no better. The
  modest one-sample *t*'s are drift, not breadth.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed (per-ticker delta negative in all 5 names), and costs only deepen the hole. You'd
  capture the same drift more cheaply by holding the index. Nothing to scale.
- **"Does the BPI forecast turns"? — BUSTED.** The scrambled-breadth placebo leaves the result
  intact (*p* = 0.974): a randomly re-timed BPI does as well as the real one, so the specific
  breadth path carries no forecasting information. The BPI is a descriptive breadth gauge, not a
  turn-forecasting strategy.
